lines.1: Today I saw Śrī herself, and I saw his golden form, shining —
lines.2: I saw the lovely radiance of the blazing sun, I saw the mighty,
lines.3: golden discus, and the curved conch resting in his hand —
lines.4: all this, today, beside my ocean-hued Lord.
lines.5: This very day I saw his sacred feet, and I have cut off my seven births.
lines.6: O Tirumāl, on whose gold-touched, mountain-broad chest the fragrant tulasī once rested,
lines.7: you who are forever seen together with Śrī —
lines.8: having found and fixed upon you, my mind has taken you as its very own companion.
lines.9: He dwells within the mind; he dwells in the waters of the great ocean; he dwells
lines.10: in the bosom of the lotus-lady, Lakshmi; his chest wears the cool tulasī — in his wrath
lines.11: he delighted in utterly destroying the enemy in battle, he of the hue of the honeyed, billowing sea —
lines.12: he is the very medicine that cures the hell that is yet to come.
lines.13: He himself is the medicine, the meaning, and the nectar —
lines.14: the flawless, red-eyed Māl, who dwelt there in fitting measure,
lines.15: who, standing, swallowed the worlds and disgorged them again, who received the water of the gift and, with three strides,
lines.16: once spanned the whole world — those are his feet.
lines.17: The hue of his feet is that of the lotus — he who once spanned the world;
lines.18: the hue of his form is that of the waters of the Milk Ocean; the hue of his crown
lines.19: is the very radiance of the blazing sun —
lines.20: such is the beauty of him who bears the full discus.
lines.21: Is it not beauty itself — for the Lord of the Discus, the hue of the ocean's waters?
lines.22: Is it not beauty, the crossing of the universe in a single stride? Is it not beauty indeed,
lines.23: that for the one who received the water of the gift in his palm, the Lotus-Born One washed his foot,
lines.24: and from those feet poured forth the waters of the Ganges?
lines.25: Come, O heart, let us worship his feet — he who measured out
lines.26: the groves bordered by the dark, roaring sea, the wealthy Lord who rides the bird,
lines.27: whose beauty there is beyond all reckoning, who is beyond all counting, who is far beyond every
lines.28: thing that is, and hard indeed for us to approach —
lines.29: Uttering his many names, crying 'O Nārāyaṇa!',
lines.30: let us worship with joined palms — come, good heart, and be one with him —
lines.31: let our eyes behold none other than Kaṇṇan, who swallowed the whole earth and spat it out again,
lines.32: who wears the cool tulasī garland murmuring with bees.
lines.33: His eyes are lotuses, his palms too are lotuses,
lines.34: and so, if one considers it, are the feet that once measured the earth —
lines.35: he of the hue of the great dark rain-cloud, he of the hue of the dark ocean's waters,
lines.36: the splendor of the great, sacred, sapphire-hued one.
lines.37: Splendor, strength, glory, beauty of form,
lines.38: spotless noble birth, and all other virtues, to speak of it all —
lines.39: they come of themselves, fittingly, to whoever utters the great name
lines.40: of him who holds the mighty right-whorled conch.
lines.41: He dwells within the four well-chanted Vedas; he is the hue of the surging,
lines.42: fragrant, roaring floodwaters; in the Milk Ocean where conches resound
lines.43: he lies upon the serpent-bed — for those who constantly proclaim him,
lines.44: he is the ocean of scripture, he of subtle, penetrating wisdom.
lines.45: Bolting fast the lock called wisdom, and shutting tight upon the five senses
lines.46: the strong door called restraint — those who forever chant the scriptures rightly
lines.47: and rightly grasp their meaning — they alone will behold, day after day,
lines.48: the true nature of the Lord, hued like the fresh, surging sea.
lines.49: Once, having received the gift of water for all the worlds, when he measured them
lines.50: with the round of his foot, the round of his crown so extended
lines.51: that it pierced through the very sky and stretched beyond the cosmic shell —
lines.52: such was Māl, who stood there as one vast, boundless form.
lines.53: Letting the mind swirl after the wrong path, loosening the arms of women in renunciation,
lines.54: to fix the mind instead upon the true path is no easy thing — but bowing
lines.55: at the feet of him who is the very substance of the four Vedas, the Lord of Venkaṭam,
lines.56: whose feet are touched by the crowns of the celestials —
lines.57: As the risen ocean's spreading waves surge and beat, adorned
lines.58: there by the jewels of Ananta's bowed hoods,
lines.59: the Lord reclines upon that serpent-couch —
lines.60: may he come and make this servant's own mind his resting-couch.
lines.61: Where the white waves come lashing in with red coral and white pearl,
lines.62: my Father is the lamp whose beauty outshines even the twilight —
lines.63: on his glorious chest rests the one lotus-lady, his beloved —
lines.64: he has gone and made his home in Tiruvallikkēṇi.
lines.65: The day that is spent on our red-eyed Māl is never a day lost —
lines.66: every one of my days will thus become a true day, forever,
lines.67: becoming a servant only at the two feet of my Father who never perishes —
lines.68: let my mouth, unforgetting, forever praise him.
lines.69: Speaking with your own mouth, becoming the dwarf Vāmana,
lines.70: O great Māl, who measured and took from Mahābali the gift of three feet of land —
lines.71: at those matchless feet of yours that once strode across the worlds, let me be your servant
lines.72: through all seven births, and grant that I may live without fear.
lines.73: Could his grace ever fail — he who once, on the banyan leaf,
lines.74: lay as an unknowing infant — for those whose minds are free of darkness,
lines.75: who offer fresh red blossoms and worship with joined hands only at his red feet,
lines.76: who stand before him utterly surrendered?
lines.77: For you, who once swallowed the worlds and spat them out again,
lines.78: to measure back that same world with just two strides — is that not a wonder indeed!
lines.79: O Tirumāl, O red-eyed, towering one, our Lord —
lines.80: tell me yourself the meaning of this.
lines.81: However much those who speak of him may speak, that alone is all that can be told —
lines.82: he who wears the fragrant tulasī garland,
lines.83: the resplendent one with the discus, the conch, the bow Śārṅga —
lines.84: such is the form of him who slew the raging demon.
lines.85: Bowing their crowned, beautiful heads, the celestials
lines.86: daily behold him, showering fragrant flowers —
lines.88: O heart, long to see him rightly, exactly as he truly is.
lines.89: He who lovingly measured out heaven and earth, whose garden-grown tulasī
lines.90: buds hum with fine-winged bees and swarms going in and out of their hollows —
lines.91: at his beautiful golden feet alone,
lines.92: my mind, entwined and bewildered with love, comes to rest.
lines.93: If one considers it, the vast earth, the great sky, the wind,
lines.94: the close-pressing fire and water — of all these he became the very form,
lines.95: he who fittingly bears the one blazing discus —
lines.96: O heart, deep as the ocean, worship daily, forever clinging to his sandalled feet.
lines.97: Is there ever any loss in worshipping him? — he who swallowed
lines.98: the whole pure-watered world, whose mouth once ate the choice butter of the thick-tressed cowherd woman,
lines.99: who subdued the seven great bulls, who remains beyond the reach
lines.100: even of the celestials — worship him, O heart, with all your devotion.
lines.101: My own humble mind, made worthy by him; the red-eyed serpent; and the place
lines.102: where he abides within the great, glorious city of Kāñchī;
lines.103: Vēṅkaṭam, Vehkā, and Vēḷukkaip-pāḍi as well —
lines.104: the wearer of the cool tulasī never departs from these.
lines.105: Who indeed has ever known grief, who has ever suffered sorrow, among those who belong to him —
lines.106: him who churned, with his own hands, the dark ocean dense as a rain-cloud,
lines.107: the primal Cause, who took his bed of repose upon the waters —
lines.109: He took his repose upon the serpent-couch; for the sake of the five Pāṇḍava brothers,
lines.110: he once brought about the fierce war of Bhārata; and — oh wonder —
lines.111: he let himself be bound, for a mere churning-stick, by the cowherd woman;
lines.112: he is the Lord who, as an infant, drank the milk of the sharp-fanged demoness.
lines.113: The Lord who drank the demoness's milk — lifting him and setting him aside,
lines.114: the cowherd woman fearlessly gave him her own breast — his fitting,
lines.115: dark and sacred body, his sweet coral mouth,
lines.116: his babbling infant speech — turn to him, and be one with him.
lines.117: Tirumāl, who has taken his abode in the ocean, in Kuḍandhai, in Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.118: and, by his own consent, in my own mind; the high, full heaven, and Pāḍagam of the Vedas,
lines.119: Ananta's shrine, and he who wears the bountiful tulasī garland —
lines.120: these are the very dwelling-places of the Lord.
lines.121: These are his temples — having rent open Hiraṇya's chest,
lines.122: he took on the form of the Man-Lion; he who reclines upon the serpent Ādiśeṣa,
lines.123: he who dwells within the four Vedas, he who received the nectar offering,
lines.124: he who shares his very form with his consort, he who abides in the Milk Ocean.
lines.125: The Milk Ocean, Vēṅkaṭam, the serpent-bed, the cool high heaven,
lines.126: the ocean of the hundred sacred texts, and the seat of the subtlest learning —
lines.127: all these, and the very minds of those who dwell steadfast in them, he took as his abode,
lines.128: he, the cowherd boy who snapped the kurundha tree.
lines.129: As a mere infant on the banyan leaf, you gently swallowed
lines.130: all the worlds in that bygone day — truly, O great Māl,
lines.131: it was you who, churning the great ocean with Mount Mandara,
lines.132: gave the celestial nectar to the dwellers of the heavens, that day.
lines.133: Was it, perhaps, the sheer effort of measuring this world that day
lines.134: which made him, having stood and sat, at last recline in the great city of Vēḷukkai?
lines.135: Behold, O heart, him of unfailing glory,
lines.136: him who, before that, had already overcome Kaṃsa.
lines.137: Eyes that long, crying 'let us see him, let us see him!' — of him who wears
lines.138: the shining garland on his broad chest, whose golden beauty the humming bees
lines.139: circle as if singing his praise —
lines.140: let us, with joined hands, sing and worship his beautiful golden feet.
lines.141: The fiery discus in his hand, the white conch from the dark ocean,
lines.142: the fierce mace, the bow Śārṅga, the blazing sword —
lines.143: such are the weapons of the wondrous Lord who measured with his own foot
lines.145: To him I have become a bound servant — he who is within all things and without them,
lines.146: he who dwells in the bitter, dark ocean's waters,
lines.147: on whose sacred chest, gleaming with a necklace strung with many gems,
lines.148: rests also the coral-lipped, lotus-born lady, Lakshmi, herself.
lines.149: He alone is his own equal; his own form is every form there is;
lines.150: he himself is the form of penance, and he himself is the very stars;
lines.151: the blazing fire, the great mountains, the eight directions —
lines.152: he is the Lord who has become the sun and moon of this universe.
lines.153: Becoming the Lord, becoming the earth, becoming the eight directions himself,
lines.154: becoming the Vedas and their inmost meaning, becoming the very sky —
lines.155: the Lord of Vēṅkaṭam, with its fitting crescent moon and its bright, resounding waterfalls,
lines.156: he exists within the very depths of the mind.
lines.157: He exists — see it, O good heart; the Supreme One
lines.158: exists forever — see it; within the very mind of those who meditate on him,
lines.159: he exists — see it: the Lord of Vēṅkaṭam, whose peaks rise so high the very sky recedes,
lines.160: whose swelling waterfalls rush down — the King who once measured the earth till it shrank before him.
lines.161: His abiding, jeweled crown stretched beyond the cosmic shell; his encircling feet
lines.162: reach every crowded grove in all eight directions; clothed in a garment
lines.163: that shimmered like lightning, he measured the worlds that day —
lines.164: the King who later held up the very mountain as an umbrella.
lines.165: Becoming a cowherd, tending the cattle herds, playing on his flute,
lines.166: mightily rending the horse-demon — the sapphire-hued one,
lines.167: resolved and took the form of the Man-Lion,
lines.168: and in his wrath tore open Hiraṇya's chest with his sharp claws.
lines.169: Felling the strong tusk of the raging, rutting elephant,
lines.170: taking the wide earth itself as his rightful treasure —
lines.171: he of the broad, garlanded chest gathers it all within his vast form:
lines.172: within that single expanse lies the whole world.
lines.173: The world, and the aeons that outlast the world, the bright, blossoming rays
lines.174: of the sun, and the red fire itself — all these he becomes; he of the fresh-gold crown
lines.175: who scatters forth his many rays —
lines.176: fix yourself, O my heart, wholly upon his paired feet.
lines.177: Where rutting elephants wander in passion with their great mates,
lines.178: and, roused to fury, lock and gore each other's tusks, and the glorious,
lines.179: spreading white tusks shed pearls upon the ground — that is Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.180: the mountain of him who, on an earlier day, bore up the very earth upon his tusk.
lines.181: Setting the great mountain upon its summit as the churning-rod, winding
lines.182: the serpent Vāsuki about it, grasping one end himself in his own hand,
lines.183: as the crest of the waves splashed water clear up to the sky's edge —
lines.184: such was the Lord who that day churned the ocean, standing there as its very support.
lines.185: O Lord who once stood and measured; O Lord who, receiving the water-gift,
lines.186: went pervading through all the worlds; O red-eyed one, who that day
lines.187: tore open the mouth of the horse-demon; O tulasī-crowned one —
lines.188: it is you, too, who tore open the very mouth of hell to save us.
lines.189: Was it not you who, receiving the water-gift, measured the world with your feet?
lines.190: Was it not you who stood and herded the cattle? Was it not you
lines.191: who tore open the great horse-demon's mouth by force, who passed between the great twin trees,
lines.192: who fought and destroyed the demons in the war of gods?
lines.193: And that you destroyed the unapproachable Hiraṇya, going straight at him;
lines.194: and that you won the great earth; and that, for Piṉṉai's sake,
lines.195: you stood before the fierce, raging bulls and stripped them of their strength —
lines.196: all this is yours, O you of the curling, roaring conch.
lines.197: Wreathed in the swaying tulasī garland, Māl of the radiant, jeweled crown,
lines.198: at the mouth of the broad mountain with its falling streams,
lines.199: in the deep, gem-clear pond, slew the great crocodile that dwelt there —
lines.200: he, of the beautiful sapphire hue.
lines.201: He it is who protected the cattle herds with the great mountain;
lines.202: he it is who felled the beautiful twin trees; he it is,
lines.203: behold, who shows us the way to that great city untouched by grief —
lines.204: he it is who, with his arrows, brought the burning of Laṅkā.
lines.205: As Rāma, he shot his arrow clean through the seven marā trees;
lines.206: the Lord shot the golden deer, for the sake of his bejeweled lady;
lines.207: he loosed his arrows so that the King of southern Laṅkā fell —
lines.208: and, taking the form of the dwarf, he strove and won the earth before Mahābali.
lines.209: Strive, O heart, and worship — in the surging-watered ocean,
lines.210: upon the banyan leaf fittingly formed, again and again, at that time,
lines.211: in the flood that had swallowed up the earth, as the wondrous infant —
lines.212: worship the feet of Māl, who wears the cool, swaying garland.
lines.213: Kicking the cart-demon with his foot, uprooting the great elephant,
lines.214: passing between the unyielding twin trees, becoming the Boar,
lines.215: and tearing open the wide earth without turning back — for him whose chest delighted
lines.216: in that lady of the earth, great indeed is his love.
lines.217: On his broad chest, mountain-wide, wearing the great pearl garland,
lines.218: as lightning flickers amid a dark cloud when it moves —
lines.219: even the lotus, humming with bees whose melody yields before it,
lines.220: shows only the hue of that Lord's own long, wide eyes.
lines.221: Some say his hue is white, some pale, some black —
lines.222: we truly cannot say what the Lord's form is; even she of boundless,
lines.223: countless virtues, the earth-goddess, herself can scarcely fathom it —
lines.224: such is the splendor of the husband of the lotus-lady.
lines.225: Appearing like lightning amid the resplendent, dark rain-clouds,
lines.226: on whose chest abundant Śrī dwells,
lines.228: fix your clear understanding upon his feet alone; be certain of it.
lines.229: Where the female monkey, sitting on the bright rock,
lines.230: gazes fondly at her mate and calls out to the shining white moon as if it were fruit, 'leap for it!' —
lines.232: the abode of him who, on an earlier day, gladly took the whole earth into his reckoning.
lines.233: I have found the true way to live: at the foot of that tall, collyrium-dark mountain,
lines.234: where his garland falls like the tumbling waterfalls, encircling all —
lines.235: the great, sacred, sapphire-hued one, our red-eyed Māl, our Lord —
lines.236: I have come to reach and unite with his feet.
lines.237: The bull-demon, the twin trees, the demoness's breast, the great terrible cart —
lines.238: he dealt with them all; passing between the trees, he ate the butter and kicked the cart,
lines.239: and, seizing a calf, he flung it at the wood-apple to bring the hidden demons down —
lines.240: and, victorious, he once gladly set the conch to his lips.
lines.241: Of old, his abodes were Vēṅkaṭam, the Milk Ocean, and Vaikuṇṭha —
lines.242: and for him who took up residence there, like another temple,
lines.243: is Vaṇ Pūṅkaḍigai, with its long, thriving groves alive with humming bees,
lines.244: the celestial abode of the ever-youthful Lord.
lines.245: Viṇṇagaram, Vehkā, Vēṅkaṭam with its spreading, wave-tossed waters,
lines.246: Maṇṇagaram, the great-mansioned Vēḷukkai, earthly Then-Kuḍandhai,
lines.248: these are the dwelling-places of him who received the water-gift in his own cupped palm.
lines.249: The matted, hanging locks and the tall crown, the bright axe and the discus,
lines.250: the coiling serpent and the golden waist-band — wondrously they appear together
lines.251: on the sacred hill, where the gathered waterfalls come rushing down —
lines.252: for my Father, the two forms unite and become one.
lines.253: The serpent, the mountain, and the ocean came together in accord,
lines.254: and, stirring, softened there and yielded up their nectar —
lines.255: was it, perhaps, the sheer weariness of that churning
lines.256: that made him lie down, sit, and stand there, at Kāñchī's Vehkā?
lines.257: There, meeting no obstacle, at the hour of twilight,
lines.258: so that Hiraṇya's body might perish, surging in fury,
lines.259: he took the form of the Man-Lion and tore it open — that very same Lord,
lines.260: in wrath, once snapped the tusk of the dark, raging elephant.
lines.261: Burning away the darkness with his radiant heat, upon the shining gems
lines.262: set in the serpent's hood, as they seemed to breathe hot breath —
lines.263: those foes who so drew his notice found their strength melt away and perished;
lines.264: that, there, was the doom that overtook them.
lines.265: There it opens and closes — the tall, beautiful lotus
lines.266: that rises from Māl's navel, there mistaking, forever,
lines.267: the radiance of his discus for the sun,
lines.268: and the white conch for the moon in the sky, gazing at them always.
lines.269: Where the monkey, seeing its own reflection in the pool's water,
lines.270: mistakes it for another monkey and shies away, then reaches out its hand
lines.271: for the ripe forest fruit — that is Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.272: the hill of him who once flung the calf at the wood-apple.
lines.273: They sing of Vēṅkaṭam simply as 'the Hill'; they wear the wondrous tulasī
lines.274: as devotedly as a woman keeps her marriage vow, upon their dark hair, like a warrior's crest —
lines.275: to bathe in the long ocean where the long-armed Māl lies reclining,
lines.276: on every day set apart for him, they go.
lines.277: Smearing its mouth with its own flowing musth, as the waterfall
lines.278: cascades down below, washing its feet in that same flow, with its trunk
lines.279: taking up a fully-blossomed flower rich with honey — toward the mighty
lines.281: such is the elephant that beholds him and bows in worship.
lines.282: Where the tusker, mistaking a cloud for a rival, raises its trunk and charges,
lines.283: where the maned lion roars and bristles,
lines.284: and the hill itself resounds with the crash — that is Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.285: the hill of him who, on a former day, took the young calf and flung it.
lines.286: Where the hill-tribe maidens, with their slender, bangled hands,
lines.287: go and play, raiding the sweet bamboo groves in triumph,
lines.288: where the very hill seems to free the shining moon from its eclipse — that is Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.289: the abode of the eternal, ever-youthful King.
lines.290: Where the seven-horsed chariot of the sun goes driving by,
lines.291: abiding in north-facing Vēṅkaṭam, inclined toward the west,
lines.292: he stood there as the Dancer — to speak only of his resounding, anklet-clad feet
lines.293: is the one true good my tongue possesses.
lines.294: Is it his own goodness that proved the true strength — or some trick of his —
lines.295: that the cruel demoness who fed him poison from her breast
lines.296: rolled upon the earth and fell? Him who drank at that fierce breast,
lines.297: the cowherd woman then took up and set her own breast to his mouth — draw near to that grace.
lines.298: Where something rubs close against the wide-horned mountain's peak,
lines.299: joined there with the bright, hare-marked, gliding white moon,
lines.300: where the fierce tiger lies in watch — that is the sacred hill of the cowherd,
lines.301: fragrant with the wild vēṅgai blossoms of the forest.
lines.302: Standing amid the mountains, bathing in the waters, standing
lines.303: amid the five fires — there is no need for any of this;
lines.304: if one offers true, fresh flowers and worships with joined hands
lines.305: him who by his own choice dwells at Vehkā, right there his evil deeds are searched out and destroyed.
lines.306: While the four-faced one, learned deeply in the scriptures, lay soundly asleep,
lines.307: he became the perfect small form, and, unseen, told out the count of days —
lines.308: and he who once counted out the many crowned heads of the sword-wielding demon —
lines.309: his ample feet alone are our true refuge.
lines.310: He who is ever our fortress, the wielder of the mighty discus,
lines.311: the strong one around whom the enemy's fury whirls in defeat —
lines.312: if he alone becomes our refuge, there is no need to ask what path, what state, what birth awaits us —
lines.313: only to meditate upon and proclaim him, the wondrous one, as the one true path.
lines.314: Becoming firm and resolved in mind, subduing the five senses, searching deeply within —
lines.315: if one turns toward him, one can shed even seven births;
lines.316: he who wears the dark, fragrant tulasī, whose form is like the swelling, roaring sea,
lines.317: whose chest is ever full — stand fast, and worship him alone.
lines.318: Bāṇāsura, lord of the bejeweled war-chariots, stood in defiance —
lines.319: and his thousand joined arms were severed, as the victorious,
lines.320: roaring discus flashed and triumphed — at the red feet of him who reclines on the serpent-couch,
lines.321: my own heart strives to reach and be one.
lines.322: Though he is beyond the mind's grasp to conceive, having found in him
lines.323: a true foothold, speak now, O my heart! When I reflect,
lines.324: the Lord stands unmoving, fixed within my very heart —
lines.325: why then does my understanding stand still, never truly searching him out?
lines.326: Through mere perception he is hard to grasp; yet, having entered the heart,
lines.327: even in that union he remains hard fully to behold —
lines.328: the Lord of the cool tulasī, thick with honey, around which the bees hum and cluster —
lines.329: where now can we go to find and behold him?
lines.330: Though the wise declare, 'he is the sweet, wondrous one,'
lines.331: and though that sweet one remains hard indeed to see —
lines.332: that same sweet one, who by his own guile took the earth and strode beyond the very heavens,
lines.333: he of the tender feet, dwells nonetheless within the depths of the heart.
lines.334: The inner meaning of the four Vedas, which truly is himself —
lines.335: though some, searching, come to realize he exists within their own heart —
lines.336: the wondrous one, whose long lotus eyes throng with bees —
lines.337: who indeed are they who have beheld him and rejoiced in song?
lines.338: Those who worship with joined hands go to his beautiful feet;
lines.339: those who, through listening, grow wise in the scriptures, attain him too —
lines.340: as the people of this earth praise and proclaim him, does it not shine forth,
lines.341: the beauty of the Father who tamed the raging bulls, for Piṉṉai's sake?
lines.342: Raising up its lightning like a beautiful banner, thundering
lines.343: of its own swift accord, appearing there —
lines.344: the dark, rain-laden sky shows, in that moment,
lines.345: the very hue of the tall Māl, beautiful as a water-laden cloud.
lines.346: As the stars blend and twinkle in the twilight, O Kaṇṇā,
lines.347: your body's blossoming beauty gleams forth like the very emerald —
lines.348: the Lord of the cool tulasī, at whose honeyed clusters the bees hum,
lines.349: that is what the evening sky reveals.
lines.350: Without doubting, asking 'is this good, is that bad' —
lines.351: worship only him whose chest bears the cool, honey-laden tulasī,
lines.352: worship only his beautiful golden feet, which stand open equally to all,
lines.353: so that every one of your past deeds may be utterly undone.
lines.354: At harvest time, where the hill-tribe farmers, their boar-drawn ploughs
lines.355: digging deep, have sown the fresh millet, and the thick-grown bamboo stalks
lines.356: rise up as if to pierce the very sky — that is Vēṅkaṭam,
lines.357: the hill that echoes with the anklets of him who, on a former day, set the sweet flute to his lips.
lines.358: As his anklets and close-worn ankle-rings rang out with every step,
lines.359: his red feet brushing against the very sky, his arms reaching
lines.360: as far as the cosmic shell — why was it, I wonder, that even the space
lines.361: encircling all eight directions was not enough for the tulasī-wearing Māl to measure the earth?
lines.362: Though he ate mud, though he drank the demoness's poisoned milk,
lines.363: nothing could harm him — yet when he swallowed the stolen butter,
lines.364: the enraged cowherd woman bound him with a small cord about his waist,
lines.365: and he, the child whom nothing can ever truly contain, let himself be bound.
lines.366: The wondrous one of great form, who is son to no one, himself becomes a son —
lines.367: and when Bāṇāsura imprisoned his own beloved grandson,
lines.368: he it was who destroyed Bāṇa's arms —
lines.369: fix yourself, O my heart, wholly upon his feet.
lines.370: Though the people of this world reflect on him, few come to true clarity —
lines.371: the great, ever-abiding Tirumāl, who gathered all the worlds within himself,
lines.372: and, a single infant upon the banyan leaf amid the roaring flood,
lines.373: lay there gently sleeping — carry him, O heart, and set him deep within.
lines.374: Kindling the radiant lamp called true understanding, I sought
lines.375: the one enshrined within, and softly, gently, I have ensnared him —
lines.376: he stood, he sat, he lay down,
lines.377: the imperishable, wondrous one, having entered my own heart.
lines.378: Entering there, resplendent, at the hour of twilight, becoming the Man-Lion,
lines.379: he tore open the body of the scornful Hiraṇya, so that it was scattered everywhere —
lines.381: and forever praise the sacred feet of that great Tirumāl.
lines.382: Let your mouths become ones that praise him — before whom the celestials
lines.383: bow low, lowering their jeweled crowns, so constantly that their gems have worn smooth —
lines.384: the bridegroom of the lady enthroned upon the lotus at his feet —
lines.385: for his own feet are themselves that very blossoming lotus.
lines.386: He from whose navel the lotus arose, the wondrous one of that beautiful,
lines.387: great form who bore that flower; he whose very hue is like the opening bloom;
lines.388: and the great one seated upon the flower, and the one of the long, matted locks —
lines.389: can even the blink of an eye truly measure such as these?
lines.390: The snow-crowned mountains, the vast sky, the wind —
lines.391: pervading them all justly, he appears and shines forth clear;
lines.392: he it is who keeps us from ever drawing near that dreaded hell,
lines.393: he who seized and tore open the mouth of the horse-demon.
lines.394: He of unfailing victory, whose weapons, eight in number, have never known defeat,
lines.395: he of the eight mighty arms — on that day, so that the savage crocodile
lines.396: in the pond might perish, he took aim and hurled his discus —
lines.397: his feet alone, first and foremost, are our true refuge.
lines.398: He who is ever our refuge, the wielder of the discus, whose broad,
lines.399: mountain-like chest bears his flourishing tulasī garland — she whom he himself embraces,
lines.400: whose long lotus-eyes, thronged with bees, flash like rare lightning in the dense monsoon sky —
lines.401: she is Śrī, throned upon the honey-laden lotus.
